subject: physics
question_text: The instantaneous speed is always equal to the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity. Why?

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Motion in a Straight Line · 4 marks

steps.label: The two definitions
lines: Instantaneous speed is the limit of
distance ÷ time as the interval shrinks:
Instantaneous velocity is the same limit of
steps.why: The two differ only in using path length Δs against displacement Δx. Everything else in the definitions is identical.
common_mistakes: Defining these as total distance over total time. That is the AVERAGE, not the instantaneous value.

recall.must_convey: That instantaneous speed is the limit of distance over time and instantaneous velocity is the limit of displacement over time, as the interval tends to zero.
accept: limit as delta t tends to zero

steps.memory_tip: Same limit, two numerators: path length Δs against displacement Δx.
steps.margin_note: Write both limits. This is the two-mark step.

steps.label: Why they agree
lines: Over a very small interval the path is
effectively straight, so the length of the path
Δs equals the magnitude of the displacement
|Δx|. In the limit the two are equal.
steps.why: A curve looks straight when you look at a small enough piece of it, so the distance travelled along it and the straight-line displacement stop differing.
common_mistakes: Saying they are equal because speed and velocity are the same thing. They are not; only their instantaneous values agree.

recall.must_convey: That over a vanishing interval the path is straight, so distance equals the magnitude of displacement.
accept: delta s equals mod delta x
reject: speed and velocity are the same

steps.memory_tip: Shrink the interval and any curve straightens. Then Δs and |Δx| are the same.
steps.margin_note: This one sentence is the actual answer to "why".

steps.label: Contrast with averages

lines.text: Average speed and |average velocity| can differ

lines: they differ whenever the direction changes,

steps.why: Naming the case where the equality fails proves the answer was understood rather than remembered.
common_mistakes: Claiming average speed always equals the magnitude of average velocity. That holds only for motion in one straight line without reversal.

recall.must_convey: That average speed and the magnitude of average velocity can differ, because distance exceeds displacement when the direction changes.

steps.memory_tip: Instantaneous: always equal. Average: equal only if the direction never reverses.
steps.margin_note: The contrast is what shows the limit was understood.

insider_note: The whole answer turns on the interval shrinking to zero. Say that and the marks follow.
